newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordan's Islamist MPs stage boycott over Israel.
newsitem.headline: Jordan's Islamist MPs stage boycott over Israel.

text.p: Jordan's Islamists briefly disrupted parliament on Wednesday and said they would boycott it in protest over the government's stance on Israel's settlement policy in Arab East Jerusalem.

"We took a decision to boycott attending the sessions of parliament in protest against the unacceptable government response to the Zionist enemy's continued measures to Judaise Jerusalem," deputy Hamza Mansour, spokesman of the Islamist Action Front (IAF), parliament's largest party, told Reuters.
The Islamist-led opposition say the government's statements of concern over Israeli plans to build 6,500 new homes for Jews in Arab East Jerusalem were not tough enough.
"We believe the minimum decision the government should take is to withdraw our ambassador and sever ties," said Mansour.

Jordan's Prime Minister Abdul-Karim al-Kabariti said last week that if the construction went ahead it would threaten the whole Middle East peace process. But he said the issue could only be solved through dialogue and that Jordan wanted to maintain "good contacts" with Israel.

Mansour said the boycott decision on Wednesday, which follows a walkout last Sunday, was binding for 15 IAF deputies and also had the support of four other leftist and independent deputies in the 80-seat parliament.

They briefly took advantage of the absence of pro-government deputies to deprive parliament of a quorum in its second session on Wednesday debating the customs law. Parliament needs 54 members to make up a quorum but less than 41 showed up.
Mansour, referring to a constant stream of official Israeli delegations visiting Jordan, said it was "offensive to people that officials should extend handshakes to the Jews."

The Moslem-led opposition, which has used the boycott tactic on rare occasions in Jordan's short parliamentary life, said it would maintain it until a tougher government stance emerged on ties with Israel.

But Hamza denied the move was an attempt to disrupt parliament, saying Islamists were only exercising a democratic right of protest which "befitted the sanctity of the cause of Jerusalem." He said the opposition had put forward a motion for a special session to debate the government's stance on Jerusalem and would attend such a session.

Asked if the boycott could be a prelude to a boycott of parliamentary elections due by year end, Hamza said: "We are talking about the present stage but we are also studying the situation constantly".

Officials say the Islamist-dominated opposition are trying to make political capital ahead of parliamentary elections, building on widespread grumbling by Jordanians of the few gains from Jordan's 1994 peace treaty with Israel.
